title: Bond selloff: The end of the beginning or beginning of the end?
gist: Oxford Economics frames the 2026 global bond selloff (US 10-year at 5.23%) as a renormalization from the 2010s negative-real-rate regime, with the latest leg driven by strong flash PMIs and rising oil. Notably, breakevens have fallen, so the selloff is led by soaring TIPS real yields; the brief questions whether pricing of four more Fed hikes is too aggressive.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics argues the global bond selloff is largely a renormalization away from the 2010s regime of deleveraging, oversaving, ZIRP, liquidity traps, QE and deflation that produced mostly negative real rates in the G7.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Structural rather than cyclical selloff implies higher-for-longer yield floor versus the 2010s; fading dips in yields may be premature.
insights.quote: the selloff in global bonds has been largely driven by a renormalization process from the 2010s

insights.claim: The renormalization of bond yields continued through September 2026, with 10-year yields reaching 5.23% in the last week of the month.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: 10-year yields above 5% mark a restrictive level that pressures duration, mortgages and equity valuations.

insights.claim: The key open question is how close the yield renormalization process is to ending, framed as whether the selloff is the 'end of the beginning or beginning of the end'.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Timing the end of renormalization is the central call for duration positioning.

insights.claim: The immediate drivers of the late-September 2026 bond selloff were strong flash PMIs combined with a renewed rise in oil prices.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Growth surprises plus oil strength are current yield catalysts; watch PMI and crude for further bond pressure.
insights.quote: The direct culprits behind last week’s bond selloff were strong flash PMIs, combined with the renewed rise in oil prices.

insights.claim: Inflation breakeven rates have fallen noticeably since early September 2026, meaning the bond market weakness has been led by soaring TIPS (real) yields rather than inflation expectations.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A real-yield-driven selloff tightens financial conditions more directly and is more threatening to long-duration assets like growth equities and gold.

insights.claim: Falling breakevens alongside rising oil prices is an unexpected combination, suggesting markets see the yield rise as a real-rate/policy story rather than an inflation scare.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Signals markets price tighter policy credibility; favors nominal/real curve trades over inflation hedges.

themes.theme: Fed hikes, fiscal laxity and equities

insights.claim: Forward markets are pricing in four additional Federal Reserve rate hikes, which Oxford Economics questions as possibly too aggressive, alongside asking whether U.S. Treasury yields are already too restrictive.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: If hike pricing is overdone, front-end duration could offer value.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics flags U.S. fiscal laxity as a factor investors must weigh for bonds and asks whether rising bond yields will spoil the equity rally.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Fiscal deficits add term-premium risk; rising yields are a key risk to equity valuations.

insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Faster BoJ normalization supports the yen and adds upward pressure to global yields via reduced Japanese capital outflows.
